body: Warehouse staff preparing the drill-bit shipment supply labour. Packing and staging are human resource inputs.
title: Mining Supplier Shutdown Window
context: Consider a mining supplier must deliver drill bits before a pit shutdown window closes. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Installing updates for a client is skilled labour deploying human resources.
body: Installing client updates is skilled human work — labour deploying know-how on the customer’s systems. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Software Support Knowledge
context: Analyze knowledge and labour in software support services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Knowledge applies only inside factories that fabricate hardware.
body: Knowledge applies in services and software support, not only inside hardware factories. The factory gate is not a knowledge border.
title: Software Support Knowledge
context: Analyze knowledge and labour in software support services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Farm operations heavy on land still need labour, equipment, and management.
body: Land-heavy farms still hire labour, run equipment, and need management. Soil alone does not operate the farm. Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: Dominant Factor Identification
context: Review identifying dominant factors without ignoring others. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Storage racks and conveyors supporting the hub are capital.
body: Storage racks and conveyors that move and hold goods are capital infrastructure for the distribution hub. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Distribution Hub Robots
context: Consider a distribution hub adds warehouse robots while keeping manual pick teams for odd-shaped orders. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Automation eliminates labour entirely in every distribution hub.
body: Automation can cut some picking tasks, but hubs still need people for odd-shaped orders, maintenance, and supervision. Labour is not eliminated in every hub.
title: Distribution Hub Robots
context: Consider a distribution hub adds warehouse robots while keeping manual pick teams for odd-shaped orders. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Insurance uses labour only because policies are intangible.
body: Insurance needs systems, premises, and finance as well as handlers. Intangible policies do not make the firm labour-only.
title: Mixed-factor Service Firms
context: Review factor combination in tertiary service businesses. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Repairs are labour-only because customers bring devices.
body: Customers bringing devices supplies the object of repair; the shop still uses tools, parts, and diagnostic technology. Repairs are not labour-only.
title: Mixed-factor Service Firms
context: Review factor combination in tertiary service businesses. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Plant managers coordinating shifts and suppliers supply entrepreneurship.
body: Plant managers who line up shifts and suppliers supply entrepreneurship — organising people and inputs around the equipment.
title: Workforce and Materials in Manufacturing
context: Review whether manufacturing can run on capital alone. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Quality inspectors monitoring batches supply skilled labour on the line.
body: Quality inspectors watching batches supply skilled labour on the line. Inspection is human resource input. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Workforce and Materials in Manufacturing
context: Review whether manufacturing can run on capital alone. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Vineyard parcels and grape production draw on land as natural resources.
body: Vineyard parcels and grape growing draw on natural resources — land in the factor sense.
title: Vineyard Land versus Barrels
context: Review land and capital distinctions in winemaking. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Fermentation knowledge applied to blending is a knowledge production factor.
body: Fermentation know-how used in blending is knowledge applied in production, sitting beside the other factors. Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: Vineyard Land versus Barrels
context: Review land and capital distinctions in winemaking. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: River water rights used for irrigation represent natural-resource land inputs.
body: River water rights for irrigation are natural-resource land inputs, not capital machinery. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Vineyard Land versus Barrels
context: Review land and capital distinctions in winemaking. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Licensed diagnostic software and repair tools represent technology in the service model.
body: Licensed diagnostic software and repair tools are technology in the service model, shaping how jobs get done. Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: A small IT-support venture Factor Bundle
context: Analyze the factor bundle in a laptop repair and software venture. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Refurbishing laptops uses spare parts inventory as capital.
body: Spare parts held for laptop refurbishing are capital inventory for the workshop. Nothing in the claim forces a stretch past ordinary classroom use of the idea.
title: A small IT-support venture Factor Bundle
context: Analyze the factor bundle in a laptop repair and software venture. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Entrepreneurship and capital are interchangeable labels for spending.
body: Entrepreneurship and capital are different factors: one organises and bears risk; the other is resources used. They are not interchangeable spending labels.
title: Entrepreneurship versus Capital Trap
context: Review traps confusing entrepreneurship with capital. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Training customers on backups applies knowledge through skilled labour.
body: Training customers on backups applies know-how through the trainer’s labour — knowledge delivered by skilled human input.
title: Knowledge in Service Firms
context: Review knowledge as a factor outside manufacturing plants. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Specialists supply entrepreneurship only, not labour.
body: Specialists supply skilled labour (and knowledge). Specialisation does not convert them into entrepreneurship-only inputs.
title: Seasonal and Permanent Labour
context: Review labour classification for seasonal and permanent workers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: A firm can deliver goods using one dominant factor without combining others.
body: Goods still need a combination of factors. One dominant input cannot carry delivery without the others that production requires.
title: Factor Combination Requirement
context: Review whether businesses can rely on a single factor. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: A winemaker illustrates combining land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship, and experience.
body: A winemaker typically shows land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship, and experience/knowledge in one agricultural–processing story.
title: Integrated Production Examples
context: Review integrated factor use across firm types. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Agricultural sites use land alone without labour or equipment.
body: Agricultural sites still need labour and equipment. Land alone does not run a harvest. One honest counterexample under the right test is enough to sink the claim.
title: Land versus Capital on One Site
context: Review land and capital distinctions on the same production site. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Mining ore is primary-sector activity while smelting metal ingots is secondary.
body: Mining pulls ore from the ground — that is primary extraction. Smelting turns ore into metal ingots, which is a manufacturing step, so it sits in the secondary sector.
title: Three-sector Model Basics
context: Review the primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors as stages from extraction through manufacturing to services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: The tertiary sector comprises services such as banking, insurance, and coaching.
body: Banking, insurance, and coaching are service activities: they do not dig raw materials or assemble physical goods. That places them in the tertiary sector.
title: Three-sector Model Basics
context: Review the primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors as stages from extraction through manufacturing to services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: A coal mine extracting ore belongs to the primary sector.
body: A coal mine taking ore from the ground is textbook primary extraction. Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: Primary Sector Activities
context: Analyze classification of primary-sector activity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Primary-sector share typically shrinks as economic development advances.
body: As development advances, farming and other primary shares usually shrink relative to industry and especially services. That pattern is the standard sector-shift story.
title: Emerging Economy Sector Mix
context: Analyze sector patterns in emerging economies. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Advanced EU economies are service-dominated despite the importance of food production.
body: Advanced EU economies are service-dominated in output shares even though food production still matters. Tertiary weight is the structural story, not a claim that farming vanished.
title: Developed EU Tertiary Share
context: Review tertiary dominance in advanced European economies. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: A seventy percent-plus service share reflects primary dominance in advanced economies.
body: A seventy-percent-plus service share is tertiary dominance, not primary dominance. Primary would be farming, fishing, mining, and forestry taking the large share.
title: Developed EU Tertiary Share
context: Review tertiary dominance in advanced European economies. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: GDP totals the monetary value of final goods and services produced within a country's borders.
body: GDP is the monetary sum of final goods and services produced within a country’s borders. The statement restates that definition.
title: Gross Domestic Product Definition
context: Review the definition of gross domestic product as a measure of overall economic activity within a country. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: GDP growth compares inflation-adjusted GDP across years.
body: GDP growth for real comparisons uses inflation-adjusted GDP across years so price rises are not mistaken for more production.
title: GDP Growth Measure
context: Analyze how GDP growth is assessed over time. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Ignoring inflation never affects growth comparisons between years.
body: Ignoring inflation does affect growth comparisons: when prices rise, nominal growth overstates real expansion. The “never affects” claim is wrong.
title: GDP Growth Measure
context: Analyze how GDP growth is assessed over time. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Exporting advice does not convert coaching into secondary manufacturing.
body: Exporting advice is a service export. It does not turn coaching into secondary manufacturing, which would require transforming materials into goods.
title: Remote Coaching Abroad
context: Consider an Estonian coach delivers remote training sessions to clients in other countries. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Because no goods cross borders, the activity cannot be counted in GDP.
body: Services produced for foreign clients can still count in GDP where the service is produced. “No goods cross borders” does not erase service output from the accounts.
title: Remote Coaching Abroad
context: Consider an Estonian coach delivers remote training sessions to clients in other countries. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Selling coaching sessions is primary extraction because trainers work from home offices.
body: Home-office coaching is tertiary service work. It is not primary extraction merely because the trainer sits at home.
title: Remote Coaching Abroad
context: Consider an Estonian coach delivers remote training sessions to clients in other countries. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Coal extraction at the mine is primary-sector activity.
body: Coal taken from the Romanian mine is primary-sector extraction. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Coal Mine and Car Plant Quarter
context: Consider a Romanian coal mine and a Graz car plant report output in the same quarter. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Every barter transaction is always fully recorded in official GDP.
body: Barter is often missed or only partly captured in official GDP. Saying every barter deal is always fully recorded overstates what the accounts catch.
title: GDP Income Coverage Critique
context: Review criticisms that GDP misses some income. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Unpaid home maintenance done by owners is always included in GDP.
body: Owner-performed unpaid home maintenance is typically outside GDP. It is not “always included.”.
title: GDP Income Coverage Critique
context: Review criticisms that GDP misses some income. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: GDP fully captures household volunteering and unpaid care in its totals.
body: Household volunteering and unpaid care are classic GDP omissions. The totals do not fully capture them. One honest counterexample under the right test is enough to sink the claim.
title: GDP Income Coverage Critique
context: Review criticisms that GDP misses some income. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Farm output and insurance services can coexist as primary and tertiary activity.
body: Wheat harvesting on the farm is primary; claims processing at the insurance cooperative is tertiary. The two activities can sit side by side in different sectors.
title: Insurance Branch and Wheat Farm
context: Consider an insurance cooperative processes claims while a nearby farm harvests wheat. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: GDP does not tell whether growth damages resources or wellbeing.
body: GDP is a money total of final output. It does not report whether that growth depleted resources or harmed wellbeing.
title: Sustainability and GDP Quality
context: Review GDP as an indicator of sustainable or high-quality growth. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Rising GDP may coincide with pollution or resource depletion.
body: GDP can climb while pollution rises or resources are drawn down. The accounts do not subtract environmental damage by default.
title: Sustainability and GDP Quality
context: Review GDP as an indicator of sustainable or high-quality growth. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Building ships from steel plate is secondary manufacturing.
body: Building ships from steel plate transforms inputs into a finished vessel. That is secondary manufacturing.
title: Port Warehouse and Shipyard
context: Consider a port warehouse stores imported steel before a shipyard welds hull sections. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Real GDP per capita rising after inflation adjustment indicates real growth.
body: When real GDP per capita rises after inflation has been stripped out, that is the usual signal of real growth in average output.
title: Clinic Expansion and Real GDP
context: Consider a Prague clinic expands while real GDP per capita rises after inflation adjustment. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Cleanup spending automatically reduces GDP because it repairs harm.
body: Cleanup and repair spending adds to measured GDP; it does not automatically reduce the total because it “repairs harm.” The accounts record the production activity.
title: Disaster Rebuild GDP Effect
context: Review how disaster recovery affects measured GDP. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Landing herring for sale is primary-sector fishing activity.
body: Landing herring for sale is commercial fishing — primary-sector extraction of a natural resource. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Fishing Fleet and Fashion Label
context: Consider a fishing fleet lands herring while a fashion label sews jackets from imported fabric. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Developing software for customers is tertiary service activity.
body: Writing software for customers is a service activity — tertiary in the three-sector model. Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: A small IT-support venture Sector Classification
context: Analyze how to classify a small IT-support venture's trading, software, and support activities. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Every downstream step from pit to machinery counts as primary because metal is natural.
body: Downstream steps after the pit — smelting, shaping, machinery production — are secondary, not primary. “Metal is natural” does not keep the whole chain in extraction.
title: Mining Pit and Smelters Chain
context: Consider a mining pit extracts ore while downstream smelters shape metal for machinery plants. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Comparing GDP across years requires adjusting for inflation to measure real growth.
body: Year-to-year GDP comparisons need inflation adjustment if you want real growth rather than a mix of output and price change.
title: Inflation-adjusted Growth
context: Analyze the role of inflation adjustment in GDP growth. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Printing the titles at a publisher's plant is secondary manufacturing.
body: Printing titles at a publisher’s plant is manufacturing — secondary-sector work. Walk through the claim's scene once — the factor or sector label does not flip mid-shift.
title: Bookstore Distribution Branch
context: Consider a bookstore branch distributes publishers' titles to local readers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Retail trade of printed titles is tertiary activity.
body: Retail trade of printed titles to local readers is tertiary distribution, not printing. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Bookstore Distribution Branch
context: Consider a bookstore branch distributes publishers' titles to local readers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Distributing publishers' titles to readers is tertiary distribution activity.
body: Distributing publishers’ titles to readers is a distribution service. That is tertiary activity. Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: Bookstore Distribution Branch
context: Consider a bookstore branch distributes publishers' titles to local readers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Cross-country data show no link between GDP and health outcomes.
body: Cross-country data typically show a positive link between GDP and health outcomes, not “no link.”.
title: Well-being Correlation
context: Review GDP correlation with health and happiness indicators. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Finishing tables for dining rooms is tertiary because buyers are households.
body: Finishing tables is fabrication — secondary. Household buyers do not push furniture making into the tertiary sector.
title: Forestry and Furniture Plant
context: Consider a forestry concession supplies logs to a furniture plant finishing dining tables. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Transforming raw materials into finished components is secondary manufacturing.
body: Turning raw materials into finished components is the definition of secondary manufacturing in this model. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Secondary Manufacturing Role
context: Review a manufacturer producing electronic components for industrial buyers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: The manufacturer is tertiary because it sells to smartphone makers, not final consumers.
body: Industrial buyers instead of final consumers do not make the manufacturer tertiary. Secondary covers intermediate goods sold to other firms as well as consumer durables.
title: Secondary Manufacturing Role
context: Review a manufacturer producing electronic components for industrial buyers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Manufacturing and after-sales service mean the entire firm is tertiary.
body: A firm can manufacture (secondary) and also run after-sales service (tertiary). That mix does not mean the entire firm is tertiary only.
title: Sector Assignment Traps
context: Review subtle sector misclassification traps. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: After-sales repair makes the entire firm tertiary only.
body: After-sales repair is tertiary service activity, but it does not force the whole firm — including any manufacturing arm — into a tertiary-only label.
title: Sector Assignment Traps
context: Review subtle sector misclassification traps. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: GDP measures production within a country's borders regardless of firm nationality.
body: GDP follows production inside the country’s borders. Firm nationality does not decide inclusion. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: GDP Border Rule
context: Analyze the geographic rule for GDP measurement. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Final goods produced domestically within a year enter GDP totals.
body: Final goods produced domestically within the year enter the GDP total for that territory.
title: GDP Border Rule
context: Analyze the geographic rule for GDP measurement. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: GDP totals value produced without automatically distinguishing harmful from beneficial output.
body: GDP adds monetary value of output. It does not automatically tag which output is harmful and which is beneficial.
title: Quality of Growth Critique
context: Review limits of GDP regarding growth quality. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Banking is secondary because it funds manufacturing clients.
body: Funding manufacturing clients is a banking service. Lending to factories does not make the bank itself secondary.
title: Banking as Tertiary
context: Review banking within the three-sector model. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Service share alone identifies every firm's sector classification.
body: An economy-wide service share does not label every firm. Individual activities still need their own sector test — extract, manufacture, or serve.
title: Service Share Measurement
context: Analyze measuring tertiary share in total output. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: GDP per capita is commonly used as an indicator of living standards.
body: GDP per capita is widely used as a rough living-standards indicator, even though it is incomplete.  Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: GDP as an Economic Activity Indicator
context: Review GDP as an overall activity indicator. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: GDP does not replace all other indicators because it misses some income sources.
body: Because GDP misses some income sources and non-market work, it does not replace every other indicator. Complementary measures still matter.
title: GDP as an Economic Activity Indicator
context: Review GDP as an overall activity indicator. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: A bookstore selling printed titles performs tertiary retail distribution.
body: A bookstore selling printed titles is retail distribution — tertiary trade. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Retail Sector Trap
context: Review traps when classifying retail activity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Warehouse pick-and-pack for e-commerce orders is classified as a tertiary logistics activity.
body: Pick-and-pack of e-commerce orders in a warehouse is logistics service work, classified as tertiary. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Retail Sector Trap
context: Review traps when classifying retail activity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Software helpdesks troubleshooting networks provide tertiary services.
body: Helpdesks that troubleshoot networks sell support services — tertiary work.
title: Software Support Sector Trap
context: Review sector traps around software support services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Writing code for clients is secondary manufacturing.
body: Writing code for clients is a software service, not secondary manufacturing of physical goods. One honest counterexample under the right test is enough to sink the claim.
title: Software Support Sector Trap
context: Review sector traps around software support services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Support is secondary because computers are manufactured products.
body: Computers being manufactured products does not pull support work into secondary manufacturing. The helpdesk sells a service.
title: Software Support Sector Trap
context: Review sector traps around software support services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: One sector label applied to a firm prevents any activity in another sector.
body: Applying one sector label to a firm does not prevent activity in another sector. Classification follows what each activity does.
title: Multi-sector Firms
context: Analyze firms operating across more than one sector. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Economic development advancing tends to raise relative tertiary output.
body: Development tending to raise relative tertiary output is the standard structural-change claim in this chapter.  Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: Output Share Shifts
context: Analyze how sector output shares shift with development. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Secondary and tertiary shares must both fall as primary share falls.
body: When the primary share falls, secondary and tertiary shares typically rise (at least one of them does), not both fall together. The claim that both must fall is backwards.
title: Output Share Shifts
context: Analyze how sector output shares shift with development. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Low GDP per capita alone defines an emerging economy's entire sector mix.
body: Low GDP per capita is one marker, but it does not by itself define an emerging economy’s entire sector mix. Sector shares still need their own reading.
title: Standard of Living Link
context: Review linking GDP per capita to living standards. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Insurance cooperatives processing claims provide tertiary services.
body: Insurance cooperatives that process claims deliver financial services — tertiary. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Insurance Sector Type
context: Review insurance within tertiary services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Underwriting and claims payment are tertiary financial services.
body: Underwriting and paying claims are tertiary financial services, not extraction or manufacturing. Nothing in the claim forces a stretch past ordinary classroom use of the idea.
title: Insurance Sector Type
context: Review insurance within tertiary services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Remote coaching sessions sold to clients are tertiary services.
body: Remote coaching sessions sold to clients are services — tertiary.
title: Coaching as Tertiary
context: Review coaching within the tertiary sector. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Coaching combined with merchandise sales can still be tertiary service delivery.
body: Merchandise sales alongside coaching do not erase the service delivery. Coaching can remain tertiary even when a few goods are sold at the desk.
title: Coaching as Tertiary
context: Review coaching within the tertiary sector. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Coaching studios renting space and paying trainers deliver tertiary services.
body: Studios that rent space and pay trainers are organised to deliver coaching services. That is tertiary activity. Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: Coaching as Tertiary
context: Review coaching within the tertiary sector. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Retail distribution of finished goods to shops is tertiary trade.
body: Retail distribution of finished goods to shops is tertiary trade, not manufacturing. That is exactly how those nouns show up when a real firm runs the mix.
title: Distribution Services
context: Review distribution and logistics as tertiary activity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Warehousing is secondary because steel will be manufactured.
body: Warehousing steel that will later be manufactured is still logistics. Future manufacturing at a plant does not make the warehouse secondary.
title: Distribution Services
context: Review distribution and logistics as tertiary activity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Forestry supplying logs to mills is primary extraction.
body: Forestry that supplies logs to mills extracts a natural resource — primary.  Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: Raw Material Extraction
context: Analyze primary-sector extraction activities. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Olive farms harvesting crops perform primary agricultural activity.
body: Olive farms harvesting crops perform primary agricultural activity.
title: Raw Material Extraction
context: Analyze primary-sector extraction activities. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Sewing is tertiary because fashion is a consumer service.
body: Sewing is garment manufacturing — secondary. Fashion as a consumer experience does not redefine sewing as a tertiary service.
title: Transforming Raw Materials
context: Review secondary-sector transformation. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: As economies develop, relative tertiary output tends to increase.
body: As economies develop, relative tertiary output tends to increase — the usual structural shift toward services.  Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: EU Tertiary Dominance
context: Review tertiary dominance in advanced EU economies. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Primary food production dominates output in rich EU states.
body: Rich EU states are service-dominated. Primary food production remains important for nutrition but does not dominate measured output.
title: EU Tertiary Dominance
context: Review tertiary dominance in advanced EU economies. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Network troubleshooting by software helpdesks counts as tertiary service activity.
body: Network troubleshooting by software helpdesks is tertiary service work. Walk through the claim's scene once — the factor or sector label does not flip mid-shift.
title: Sector Trap Software Support
context: Review sector traps around software support. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Manufacturing devices and supporting them can span secondary and tertiary activity.
body: Making devices is secondary; supporting them is tertiary. One business story can span both sectors.  Nothing in the claim forces a stretch past ordinary classroom use of the idea.
title: Sector Trap Software Support
context: Review sector traps around software support. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: GDP measures final domestic production and supports growth comparisons when inflation-adjusted.
body: GDP measures final domestic production and, when inflation-adjusted, supports real growth comparisons across years.
title: Sector and GDP Synthesis
context: Review integrated sector and GDP claims. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Strong customer demand alone guarantees profit regardless of expenses.
body: Profit orientation centres on revenue relative to costs. Strong customer demand is the sales-side force in that comparison for the profit-oriented firm in this case set.
title: Profit-oriented Basics
context: Review how profit-oriented businesses relate revenues to costs and expenses. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Profit means matching expenses exactly while ignoring any surplus.
body: Matching expenses exactly and ignoring any surplus describes break-even, not profit. Profit is the surplus when revenue exceeds costs.
title: Profit-oriented Basics
context: Review how profit-oriented businesses relate revenues to costs and expenses. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Profit emerges when revenue exceeds total costs in a period.
body: When revenue exceeds total costs in a period, the difference is profit. Nothing in the claim forces a stretch past ordinary classroom use of the idea.
title: Revenue versus Costs
context: Analyze the revenue-versus-cost relationship in profit orientation. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Not-for-profit status means the organisation may ignore funding entirely.
body: Not-for-profit status does not mean the organisation can ignore funding. Relief still needs donations, grants, or other inflows to operate.
title: Disaster Relief Funding
context: Consider a humanitarian NPO collecting donations before dispatching flood-relief kits to affected towns. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Dispatching kits without prior inflows is typical NPO practice.
body: Dispatching kits without prior inflows is not typical NPO practice. Organisations usually raise funds before or alongside distribution so supplies can be bought and shipped.
title: Disaster Relief Funding
context: Consider a humanitarian NPO collecting donations before dispatching flood-relief kits to affected towns. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Repair shops reinvesting profit into diagnostic tools show commercial reinvestment.
body: A repair shop that ploughs profit into diagnostic tools is a clear commercial reinvestment example. Exam markers reward that definition fit, not a dramatic side story.
title: Profit Reinvestment
context: Review reinvestment of profit in commercial firms. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Retirement or long-term illness of the sole proprietor may create continuity problems for the business.
body: Continuity hangs on one person’s capacity to own and manage. Retirement or long-term illness can interrupt trading unless ownership and control are formally transferred.
title: Sole Proprietorship Ownership and Management
context: Analyze how a sole proprietorship concentrates ownership and operational control in a single individual. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: If the sole proprietor needs support, he or she can hire personnel while still bearing the central management role.
body: When workload exceeds one pair of hands, the proprietor may hire personnel. Extra staff expand capacity, yet the owner keeps the central management role and the associated risk.
title: Legal Status and Tax Treatment
context: Review the legal and fiscal position of a sole proprietorship compared with incorporated business forms. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: The sole proprietor may hire personnel when additional support is required to run the business.
body: When workload exceeds one pair of hands, the proprietor may hire personnel. Extra staff expand capacity, yet the owner keeps the central management role and the associated risk.
title: Single Owner Control and Staffing
context: Analyze management authority within a sole proprietorship when the owner employs assistants for daily operations. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: The sole proprietor can make all management decisions and does not necessarily have to consider other opinions.
body: Decision rights sit undivided with the sole proprietor. Helpful opinions from staff stay optional — there is no co-owner veto the owner must clear before acting.
title: Single Owner Control and Staffing
context: Analyze management authority within a sole proprietorship when the owner employs assistants for daily operations. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Continuity of the business may be disrupted when the sole proprietor cannot continue managing due to long-term illness.
body: Continuity hangs on one person’s capacity to own and manage. Retirement or long-term illness can interrupt trading unless ownership and control are formally transferred.
title: Single Owner Control and Staffing
context: Analyze management authority within a sole proprietorship when the owner employs assistants for daily operations. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Because one person owns and manages the firm, succession planning is always simpler than in structures with transferable shares.
body: Automatic unchanged succession without a transfer arrangement is a myth. Employees cannot legally assume ownership merely by keeping the lights on.
title: Continuity Risk and Decision Authority
context: Consider operational continuity when a sole trader plans retirement after years of running a local repair workshop. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: The management of the business largely depends on the sole proprietor, who retains the most important decision rights.
body: Decision rights sit undivided with the sole proprietor. Helpful opinions from staff stay optional — there is no co-owner veto the owner must clear before acting.
title: Continuity Risk and Decision Authority
context: Consider operational continuity when a sole trader plans retirement after years of running a local repair workshop. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: If the sole proprietor needs support, personnel may be hired while the proprietor retains key management decisions.
body: When workload exceeds one pair of hands, the proprietor may hire personnel. Extra staff expand capacity, yet the owner keeps the central management role and the associated risk.
title: Core Features of Sole Trader Businesses
context: Analyze the defining characteristics of sole proprietorship as described in business ownership theory. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Continuity problems may arise if the sole proprietor suffers a long-term illness or wishes to retire.
body: Continuity hangs on one person’s capacity to own and manage. Retirement or long-term illness can interrupt trading unless ownership and control are formally transferred.
title: Legal Personality and Liability Distinctions
context: Review distinctions between unincorporated sole traders and incorporated companies regarding legal status and creditor protection. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: The sole proprietor can make all management decisions without necessarily consulting other owners.
body: Decision rights sit undivided with the sole proprietor. Helpful opinions from staff stay optional — there is no co-owner veto the owner must clear before acting.
title: Management Concentration and Risk Bearing
context: Consider a freelance designer operating as a sole proprietorship who occasionally contracts administrative help. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Even when administrative tasks are delegated, the proprietor retains authority over the most important management decisions.
body: Decision rights sit undivided with the sole proprietor. Helpful opinions from staff stay optional — there is no co-owner veto the owner must clear before acting.
title: Management Concentration and Risk Bearing
context: Consider a freelance designer operating as a sole proprietorship who occasionally contracts administrative help. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: One person owns, manages, and runs the business while retaining the most important decision authority.
body: Decision rights sit undivided with the sole proprietor. Helpful opinions from staff stay optional — there is no co-owner veto the owner must clear before acting.
title: Integrated Sole Trader Profile
context: Review the combined legal, managerial, and fiscal profile of a typical sole proprietorship. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Property used as mortgage collateral for a long-term bank loan automatically incorporates the sole proprietorship as a limited company.
body: Collateral helps the lender but does not magically exempt every other private asset from residual claims. A mortgage story also does not redefine ordinary short-term trade terms.
title: Mortgage Collateral and Repayment Duties
context: Review long-term borrowing secured against property owned by a sole proprietor. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: The sole proprietor can hire personnel when support is needed to operate the business.
body: When workload exceeds one pair of hands, the proprietor may hire personnel. Extra staff expand capacity, yet the owner keeps the central management role and the associated risk.
title: Management Retention Despite Staffing
context: Consider a retail sole proprietorship where the owner employs sales staff for daily customer service. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Management of the business largely depends on the sole proprietor even when staff are present.
body: When workload exceeds one pair of hands, the proprietor may hire personnel. Extra staff expand capacity, yet the owner keeps the central management role and the associated risk.
title: Management Retention Despite Staffing
context: Consider a retail sole proprietorship where the owner employs sales staff for daily customer service. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Continuity problems may occur if the sole proprietor suffers a long-term illness.
body: Continuity hangs on one person’s capacity to own and manage. Retirement or long-term illness can interrupt trading unless ownership and control are formally transferred.
title: Succession and Illness Continuity
context: Analyze continuity risks when a sole proprietor faces prolonged absence from management duties. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Retirement plans of the sole proprietor can create continuity problems for the business.
body: Continuity hangs on one person’s capacity to own and manage. Retirement or long-term illness can interrupt trading unless ownership and control are formally transferred.
title: Succession and Illness Continuity
context: Analyze continuity risks when a sole proprietor faces prolonged absence from management duties. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: If two or more persons jointly found a business, that business is called a partnership.
body: Joint founding by two or more persons is what makes the business a partnership. One owner alone, even with a full payroll, is still sole trading.
title: Partnership Formation and Agreement Essentials
context: Consider two consultants who jointly found a business and draft a partnership agreement covering ownership shares, profit division, and decision rights. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Two or more persons who jointly found a business create what is economically termed a partnership.
body: Joint founding by two or more persons is what makes the business a partnership. One owner alone, even with a full payroll, is still sole trading.
title: Partnership Finance Compared With Sole Trading
context: Consider a neighbourhood bakery founded by two partners who pool savings and seek a bank loan for equipment. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Managers of a corporation need not own a share of the business.
body: Shareholders need not run day-to-day operations, and managers need not own shares. Ownership and operational control can separate through boards and executives.
title: Corporations as Legal Persons
context: Review how incorporated businesses obtain separate legal personality and the rights that follow from that status. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Exchange is irrelevant to whether a computer counts as a product if customers desire it strongly enough.
body: Exchange is not irrelevant. Strong desire without a trade still leaves you short of a marketed product. The computer must be exchanged with a customer.
title: Scope Beyond Tangible Goods
context: Consider a wholesale stationery supplier that sells printers to corporate offices while also stocking identical models for walk-in household buyers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: A catering tray transferred internally between branches of one corporation remains a marketed product.
body: Moving a catering tray between branches of one corporation is internal transfer, not external customer exchange. It does not remain a marketed product under the exchange test.
title: Inter-Business Service Products
context: Review how customer wishes and needs frame the purpose of goods and services offered as products. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Satisfaction objectives aim to convert first-time buyers into customers who return.
body: Satisfaction objectives aim to convert first-time buyers into customers who return. The goal is not a single smile at checkout but a plausible path to the next purchase.
title: Interrelated Marketing Goals
context: Analyze how customer satisfaction interrelates with other marketing objectives such as sales and loyalty. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: If a product fails to meet needs, marketing objectives around sales growth become harder to reach.
body: If a product fails to meet needs, sales-growth objectives get much harder. Volume targets fight uphill when buyers leave unhappy after trial.
title: Satisfaction and Repeat Purchase
context: Analyze why building a brand supports the creation of a unique selling proposition. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Marketing objectives treat satisfaction as separate from loyalty with no connection.
body: Marketing does not treat satisfaction as sealed off from loyalty with no link. Loyalty outcomes depend on satisfactory prior experience in the chapter’s framework.
title: Relative Market Importance
context: Analyze the relationship between higher sales figures and profitability within stated limitations. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Satisfied customers never buy complementary products from the same firm.
body: Satisfied customers often do buy complementary products from the same firm. Contentment opens cross-sell; it does not seal buyers into a single SKU forever.
title: Profit Reinvestment Rationale
context: Consider a boutique hotel group emphasising personalised service, measuring guest review scores, and aiming to raise occupancy revenue. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Dissatisfied customers still generate loyal behaviour if enrolled in a rewards scheme.
body: Rewards enrolment does not turn dissatisfied buyers into truly loyal ones. Points cannot paper over a product that failed the customer’s wishes.
title: Perceived Product Uniqueness
context: Analyze how retained profit from higher sales can be reinvested in the business. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: A satisfied customer will never switch to a rival with a stronger USP.
body: Even a satisfied customer may switch if a rival offers a stronger USP. Contentment helps retention; it is not an unbreakable lock against better-perceived alternatives.
title: Share Maintenance Strategies
context: Consider a regional bakery that tracks repeat purchases, complaint rates, and promotional responses while setting annual marketing targets. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Satisfied customers are more receptive to extensions of a product line from the same business.
body: Satisfied customers are more receptive to extensions of a product line from the same business because trust from prior experience carries over to the next SKU.
title: Sales-Profit Relationship Limits
context: Review why businesses analyse customer wishes and needs before defining marketing objectives. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Customers cannot perceive a USP when products are functionally similar.
body: Customers cannot perceive a USP when products are functionally similar.
title: Market Position Relative to Rivals
context: Consider a coffee roaster building brand recognition, measuring customer satisfaction scores, and targeting a larger share of the specialty segment. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: A unique selling proposition guarantees unlimited market share without further effort.
body:
A unique selling proposition guarantees unlimited market share without further effort.

Applied to the coffee roaster, that check keeps the teaching concrete.
title: Market Position Relative to Rivals
context: Consider a coffee roaster building brand recognition, measuring customer satisfaction scores, and targeting a larger share of the specialty segment. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Promotion cannot change customer perception of uniqueness once the product is launched.
body: Promotion can reshape perceived uniqueness after launch. Messaging and packaging refreshes keep working on how customers classify the offer — uniqueness is not frozen on day one.
title: Higher Sales and Profit Link
context: Analyze how a clear unique selling proposition helps attract many loyal customers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Relative importance in the market is shown by advertising spend, not share.
body: Relative importance is what share is designed to indicate, not advertising spend alone. Heavy media budgets can still leave a firm mid-pack if rivals outsell it.
title: Satisfaction Supporting Sales
context: Consider a furniture retailer that surveys post-purchase satisfaction, promotes a craftsmanship guarantee, and aims to grow regional sales volume. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Gaining market share means the total market size must shrink.
body: Gaining market share does not require the total market to shrink. Firms can take a larger portion while the pie grows. Forcing shrinkage as a precondition invents a rule.
title: Distinct Identity in Crowded Markets
context: Review customer satisfaction surveys as inputs to marketing objective setting. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Market-oriented businesses define specifications first and only later consider whether buyers want those features.
body: Contrast the true category with the trap the statement falls into.
title: Focus on Features or Customer Needs
context: Analyze the contrast between focusing on product features and focusing on customers' needs and wants in marketing orientation. Evaluate the following economic assertions:

statement: Buying-behaviour records cannot inform tailored offers because preferences never change after one purchase.
title: Personal Data Trade-Offs in Loyalty Schemes
